social capital is not only a resource, but also a tool that is actively used by members of student organisations to advance their careers and social standing.
the corps’ social space is a complex and layered one.
women’s social networks are indeed segregated, and their divisions are dependent on previously acquired cultural, economic and symbolic capital.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women’s ability to navigate the corps’ social space is determined by their ability to perform ‘respectable’ femininity and by their previously acquired social capital.

women are able to move through social networks and use their social capital in selective ways, however, their ability to do so is dependent on the enactment and achievement, as well as the recognition of ‘proper’ feminine behaviour.
women are not passive victims in the corps’ space but actively use the social capital they have gained from their membership to advance their careers and to achieve their personal goals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the corps is a highly stratified space that reproduces social inequalities and hierarchies.
the social networks that form at traditional student organisations are not segregated by gender.
women’s social networks are not only shaped by gender, but also by class and other intersecting identities, which should be considered in future research on women’s social capital.
